title: Garder la maison ensemble  (Holding the Fort Together)

segments.t: Back at the Paris office, Herve returns flustered, only to find Noemie crying after giving up her travel ticket to Mathias's wife. Recognizing her heartbreak over Mathias, Herve offers comforting words and decides to stay in Paris with her so they can hold down the fort together. Listen to the scene in French first.
C'est horrible, vraiment horrible!
Tu n'es pas dans le train?
Non, je n'y vais plus.
Mais pourquoi ce changement soudain?
Le moment était vraiment mal choisi.
Tu peux y aller si tu veux.
Je garderai la maison tout seul.
Tu es sûre de ton choix?
Tu as prévenu Mathias?
J'ai dit que j'étais malade.
Tu pleures, Noémie?
C'est à cause d'un homme?
Oui, mais je vais m'en remettre.
Je vais rester ici aussi.
Merci pour ton soutien, Hervé!
Let's walk through the conversation step by step.
C'est horrible, vraiment horrible!
'It is horrible, truly horrible!' Spelled identically in French and English, 'horrible' is a dramatic cognate except that the leading 'h' is completely silent!
Tu n'es pas dans le train?
'Are you not on the train?' Where English says 'on the train,' French puts travelers 'in the train.'
Non, je n'y vais plus.
'No, I am not going anymore.' That tiny 'there' stand-in IS mandatory before 'go' in French—you can never leave 'I go' dangling without a destination!
Mais pourquoi ce changement soudain?
'But why this sudden change?' Skipping the verb after 'but why' creates a natural surprised fragment, with 'sudden' placed after 'change' in French.
Le moment était vraiment mal choisi.
'The timing was really poorly chosen.' Literally 'the moment was really badly chosen,' where 'moment' covers what English calls 'timing.'
Tu peux y aller si tu veux.
'You can go if you want.' Again that little destination stand-in meaning 'there' tucks right before 'to go'—literally 'you can there go.'
Je garderai la maison tout seul.
'I will hold down the fort all alone.' Literally 'guard the house,' a cozy domestic idiom in French for minding the office while everyone is away.
Tu es sûre de ton choix?
'Are you sure of your choice?' Casual 'you' plus 'sure of' links directly with 'of' just as in English.
Tu as prévenu Mathias?
'Have you warned Mathias?' Built from 'come' and 'before,' that action in French means both 'warn' and 'let someone know in advance.'
J'ai dit que j'étais malade.
'I said that I was sick.' Unlike English, which can drop 'that' in 'I said I was sick,' French NEVER omits the bridge 'that' between two clauses!
Tu pleures, Noémie?
'Are you crying, Noemie?' Just two words plus her name—rising intonation turns casual 'you cry' into a gentle, concerned question in French.
C'est à cause d'un homme?
'Is it because of a man?' Literally 'at cause of a man,' this handy three-word preposition chunk expresses 'because of.'
Oui, mais je vais m'en remettre.
'Yes, but I will get over it.' Literally 'put myself back from it,' this expressive chunk is what you'd say for recovering from illness, shock, or heartbreak.
Je vais rester ici aussi.
'I will stay here too.' Watch out for a classic false friend: in French, 'rest'-lookalike ALWAYS means 'stay' or 'remain,' never 'relax'!
Merci pour ton soutien, Hervé!

'Thank you for your support, Herve!' Built from 'hold under,' the noun here literally pictures someone propping you up from beneath—'support.' Now let's listen to the whole scene again at normal speed, and see how much more you catch.
C'est horrible, vraiment horrible!
Tu n'es pas dans le train?
Non, je n'y vais plus.
Mais pourquoi ce changement soudain?
Le moment était vraiment mal choisi.
Tu peux y aller si tu veux.
Je garderai la maison tout seul.
Tu es sûre de ton choix?
Tu as prévenu Mathias?
J'ai dit que j'étais malade.
Tu pleures, Noémie?
C'est à cause d'un homme?
Oui, mais je vais m'en remettre.
Je vais rester ici aussi.
Merci pour ton soutien, Hervé!
Comforting a tearful Noemie over her secret heartbreak, Herve decides to stay behind in Paris so they can look after the office together. See you next time!
Bonne journée!
